title: Module overview
body: This module develops the operational and geometric foundations of curved spacetime. The equivalence principle, local free fall, tidal gravity, the metric and its inverse and volume structures, line elements, proper time, null curves, causal structure, local flatness, and signature conventions establish the framework used throughout GR.

title: Module overview
body: This module progresses from comparing vectors at neighbouring events to describing free motion and tidal separation. Connections, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivatives, compatibility and torsion, parallel transport, geodesics and their variational equation, four-velocity, four-acceleration, and geodesic deviation form one connected account.

title: Module overview
body: This module constructs the hierarchy from Riemann curvature through the Ricci, scalar, and Einstein tensors. The Bianchi identity and curvature invariants provide consistency and diagnostics, while the Einstein-Hilbert action bridges curvature scalars to gravitational dynamics.

title: Module overview
body: This module explains how matter sources geometry and how Einstein's equations are constrained and specialised. Stress-energy, fluid matter, energy conditions and conservation lead to the field equations, cosmological term, matter variation, and trace-reversed and vacuum forms.

title: Module overview
body: This module connects full general relativity to Newtonian gravity, classical observations, and weak radiation. Weak metric perturbations, Newtonian and post-Newtonian limits, gravitational redshift, light deflection, perihelion precession, and gravitational waves show how measurable corrections and propagating tidal effects emerge from the theory.

title: Module overview
body: This module develops the central exact vacuum geometry around a spherical mass. The Schwarzschild metric and radius lead to horizons, the distinction between coordinate and curvature singularities, and an effective-potential description of timelike and null orbits.

title: Module overview
body: A curved space need not have one preferred global coordinate system. It can be described by overlapping local charts, while scalars, curves, tangent vectors, and covectors describe quantities whose meaning does not depend on any one chart. The terrain survey below supplies one shared example for the six concepts in this module.

title: The kame-and-kettle survey
body: A group of soil scientists studies a strongly undulating landscape while insisting on treating the ground as a two-dimensional surface. Each scientist takes a small overlapping patch and places a reproducibly aligned rigid board tangent to the ground at a reference point. The board carries a straight two-dimensional grid, but its scale, orientation, and even the angle between its axes may differ from every other board. Nearby ground points are assigned board coordinates by a smooth one-to-one projection. The patch must be small enough that this projection remains unambiguous and nonsingular; the board approximates local geometry but does not make the curved ground flat. Neighbouring scientists compare the pegs in their overlaps and agree smooth rules for converting one pair of coordinates into another. They measure surface temperature \(T\), the direction and surface length of grass growth \(G\), and an intrinsic curvature estimate \(K\) at many pegged points. A mobile temperature probe also follows a route through several patches. At the club hut a mathematician shows how their incompatible-looking spreadsheets describe one surface and one set of physical measurements.

title: The mathematician's dictionary
body: The complete terrain is a manifold \(M\). One scientist's region and board labelling form a coordinate chart \((U_i,x_i)\). An agreed conversion on an overlap is a coordinate transformation. The mobile probe follows a parametrized curve \(\gamma(t)\); when time is included in the model, its complete history is a worldline. Its instantaneous velocity and the grass-growth direction are tangent vectors. Temperature and the already measured curvature estimate are scalar fields, \(T:M\rightarrow\mathbb R\) and \(K:M\rightarrow\mathbb R\). Their differentials \(dT\) and \(dK\) are covector fields: linear rules that measure how those scalars change along a chosen tangent direction.

title: One coordinate-independent measurement
body: If the probe has tangent velocity \(\dot\gamma(t)\), its rate of temperature change through a time-independent surface field is \[\frac{d}{dt}T(\gamma(t))=dT_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\dot\gamma(t)\bigr)=\left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x^i}\right|_{\gamma(t)}\frac{dx^i}{dt}.\] Likewise, \(dT(G)\) says whether grass grows locally toward warmer ground, colder ground, or along an isotherm. Vector components and covector components change oppositely between boards, so each pairing gives the same scalar answer in every scientist's coordinates.

title: Looking ahead: metric and curvature
body: Coordinates label the ground but do not by themselves determine physical lengths, angles, geodesics, or curvature. Those require a metric, which is developed later. For this module the scientists' curvature estimate is simply treated as a measured scalar \(K(p)\). One possible intrinsic estimate uses a small geodesic circle of surface radius \(r\) and circumference \(C(r)\): \[K(p)\simeq\frac{6}{r^2}\left(1-\frac{C(r)}{2\pi r}\right).\] Several radii and an extrapolation toward \(r=0\) are needed for a careful point estimate. This previews later geometry without making curvature part of the present module's promised machinery.

title: Module overview
body: This module collects the reusable tensor notation needed by GR and later physics topics. Tensor fields, index conventions, and transformation laws explain how equations can use coordinate components while still making coordinate-independent statements.

title: Module overview
body: This module unites the physical postulates of special relativity with their flat-spacetime geometry. Inertial frames, events, locality, the metric, invariant interval, Lorentz transformations, light cones, diagrams, and Lorentz invariance establish the common structure required by the rest of the SR atlas.

title: Module overview
body: This module develops relativistic particle kinematics and mechanics. Proper time and four-vectors lead through position and velocity to four-momentum and mass-energy equivalence, forming one compact derivational chain grounded in spacetime geometry.

title: Module overview
body: This module introduces the action-based machinery shared by relativistic mechanics and field theory. Lagrangians, Euler-Lagrange equations, canonical and Hamiltonian descriptions, scalar and vector fields, field Lagrangians, and field equations provide a reusable language for dynamics.

title: Module overview
body: This module develops the covariant electromagnetic field, its gauge description, its interaction with charged matter, and its local energy-momentum content. Potentials and the field tensor connect electric and magnetic fields to gauge freedom, minimal coupling, the Lorentz force, stress-energy, energy density, and momentum flow.

title: Module overview
body: This module follows relativistic fields from symmetry and equations of motion to conserved currents, propagation, and radiation. Noether's theorem, four-current, Maxwell's equations, charge and energy-momentum conservation, wave dynamics, and radiation reaction show how local field laws produce observable transport and back-reaction.
